analysis.one_liner: Lists four toxic "forever chemicals" (PFAS) as hazardous air pollutants the EPA must regulate.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in October 2021, it sat there until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written four specific "forever chemicals" — including PFOA, PFOS, PFBS, and GenX chemicals — into the Clean Air Act's list of hazardous air pollutants [S3]. That listing would require the EPA to regulate industrial sources that emit them, set emission standards within five years, and develop better ways to measure PFAS in the air [S3]. PFAS are man-made chemicals linked in the CRS summary to possible adverse human health effects [S2]. The bill was introduced by Sen. Padilla with six Democratic cosponsors, referred to the Senate environment committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near industrial facilities that emit PFAS into the air, and more broadly anyone exposed to airborne PFAS, would gain enforceable federal emission limits and better monitoring. State and local health agencies would also benefit from standardized federal measurement and reporting methods.

how_it_helps.text: It listed specific PFAS, including PFOA, PFOS, PFBS, and GenX chemicals, as hazardous air pollutants under the Clean Air Act, covering 187 toxic substances already regulated under that program's framework [S2][S3].

It required the EPA to add the source categories emitting these substances to its regulatory list within two years and to finalize emission standards for them within five years, creating enforceable federal limits where PFAS air emissions are currently unregulated as hazardous air pollutants [S3].

It required the EPA to develop and improve testing and air-measurement methods so that PFAS emissions can be identified, detected, and reported, and directed the EPA to decide within five years whether to list additional PFAS beyond the initial four [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and other industrial facilities that emit PFAS would pay for emission controls, monitoring, and reporting. Some of those costs could show up in prices for products that use these chemicals.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains a savings clause: the EPA could not enforce the new PFAS listings until emission regulations were finalized, which the bill allowed up to five years after enactment — so no new limits would bite for years [S3].

Compliance with new hazardous air pollutant standards would impose costs on chemical plants and other industrial emitters, and those costs can be passed through to prices or lead some facilities to shift production rather than cut emissions [S3].
The bill addressed air emissions only; PFAS contamination of water and soil, the pathway in many contaminated communities, would have needed separate action [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — enforceable limits on toxic PFAS air emissions near fenceline communities — is real and the bill was modest in scope: it listed four well-studied PFAS and gave the EPA up to five years to write standards, with funding for better measurement methods. The honest cost is compliance spending by chemical plants and other industrial emitters, which could push some costs into prices. The design drawback is the savings clause: no enforcement until standards are finalized years later, and a slow pace that gives industry time to adjust or shift to substitutes. On balance a low-cost, targeted public-health measure, and its death left the pollution unaddressed by this route.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate environment committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Padilla introduced the bill on October 19, 2021; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, the same day [S1][S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred; the bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].
The bill had six Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support in a Senate where Republicans held 50 seats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers and other industrial facilities that emit PFAS are better off: they face no new federal air-emission standards for these substances, and the public continues to live with unregulated PFAS air pollution.

for.name: Sen. Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

for.name: 6 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Senate cosponsors (Shaheen, Gillibrand, Feinstein, Hassan, Blumenthal, and Padilla)

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but the bill never reached a vote, so the record shows no party split on the merits — only a single-party sponsorship list [S4].

industries.note: Plants that make or use PFOA, PFOS, PFBS, and GenX chemicals would face Clean Air Act hazardous-emission standards, requiring emission controls, monitoring, and reporting they do not face today. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against the health of people living near those facilities.

industries.industry: Industrial facilities emitting PFAS (e.g., manufacturers, coating and semiconductor operations)
industries.note: Any facility whose processes release these substances would have been swept into a source category and required to meet emission standards within five years, adding compliance costs. Communities near those facilities would get reduced exposure to toxic air.
